“Class is not simply about income,” Pierre Bourdieu argued, and this observation cuts to the heart of understanding social stratification. Beyond financial wealth, stratification operates through cultural capital – the knowledge, skills, habits, and tastes that signal social status – and social capital – the networks of relationships that provide access to opportunities. Someone from a privileged background possesses not only financial resources but also an understanding of how systems work, the ability to navigate elite spaces, and connections that open doors. These forms of capital are often invisible, yet they wield immense power in shaping life trajectories. Addressing stratification, therefore, requires more than just economic redistribution; it demands a leveling of the playing field in terms of cultural and social access.
